<em>Ce reportage utilise un pronom non b: This report uses a non-binary pronoun in the original French: “iel.” In English, we use “they.” This is done to respect and recognize each individual’s gender identity. The use of non-binary pronouns is increasingly common and aims to include people who do not identify strictly as men or women. However, French grammar does not yet allow for gender-neutral agreement and conjugation. With the permission of the person interviewed, we therefore opted for feminine agreement in the French version. We wish to underline our commitment to inclusion and to respect for gender diversity, and we hope this helps create a more inclusive space for all readers.
Juin 2023. Le dernier jour du printemps: June 2023. The last day of spring fades gracefully, making way for the summer solstice on the horizon. The blazing sun sets the streets aflame, while shops, restaurants and the city itself are adorned with a myriad of rainbows, brilliantly celebrating Pride month. As June takes its bow, we meet Valentina, who shares their story as a queer, Black person in exile, with experiences that are often forgotten, even eclipsed, by the image we have of Canada as a welcoming land.

<strong>À la bibliothèque, à la recherch: At the library, searching for the word “lesbian”
« J’ai pris conscience de ma différence: “I became aware of my difference at the age of 10, but I kept the feeling inside me that something was wrong, without ever daring to talk about it to anyone,” Valentina tells us. As a child, they believed they should have been born a boy instead of a girl, since they were attracted to women. They were so convinced of this that, growing up, they were persuaded it was their mother’s intense desire for a daughter that had upended their destiny.
Aujourd’hui, à l’âge de 28 ans, Valentin: Today, at 28, Valentina describes themself as a non-binary, Black, African person. Having grown up in their native Nigeria, they say they didn’t even have the words to describe their identity, their experience: “The first time I heard the word ‘lesbian,’ it was when I pushed away a classmate, and he insulted me by calling me a lesbian.”
À 15 ans, Valentina, se rend à la biblio: At 15, Valentina goes to the school library of their religious boarding school to look up the meaning of the word. That’s where they find themself, where they identify for the first time. “But even though I had never heard that word before, I knew it was considered wrong, even if no one talked about it openly,” they explain. So the teenager turns to the website Tumblr. To their great surprise, the platform’s users already seem to know what a lesbian was, and many of them were part of the queer community. “That’s when I started meeting, online, a number of people who shared this experience. Ironically, most of them lived in Canada, where they could live their sexual identity openly and safely. So as I grew up, I nurtured the dream of going to Canada,” says Valentina.
À la suite de cet incident, Valentina se: After this incident, Valentina confides in a close friend, Marie, whom they met at boarding school. Their friendship turns into a secret relationship, although neither of them called it that or spoke about what they felt and what they were to each other. “We would wake up at 3 a.m. to take our showers because everyone showered at 6 in the morning. Once, while sneaking around, we almost got caught and Marie pushed me against the wall and a tile broke against my elbow. I was bleeding everywhere, but we couldn’t tell anyone,” says Valentina, smiling as they show the scar from that wound. “We never put a name to what we were, and besides, we both had a boyfriend,” Valentina continues, looking at their hands.
Iel prend un moment et replonge dans ses: They take a moment and dive back into their teenage memories: “I remember Marie slipping into my bed at night, we slept together. Our only consolation, with regard to religion and society more broadly, was that we didn’t do anything sexual, so nothing that bad… we kissed and we laughed, that’s all,” they say, with a hint of nostalgia.
Alors que ses études secondaires à l’int: As their secondary studies at the boarding school come to an end, Valentina decides to pursue studies abroad in order to leave Nigeria. After a mountain of paperwork and exams, they leave their native country for Ontario. “I arrived in Canada in January 2013, I was 17. After six months of preparatory school, I applied to architecture school, and I started my bachelor’s degree,” explains the architect.
Un an après l’arrivée de Valentina au Ca: A year after Valentina’s arrival in Canada, then Nigerian president Goodluck Jonathan signs a law criminalizing homosexual relationships. A law that will keep Valentina from returning to their country. “Before, homosexuality wasn’t accepted, but it wasn’t criminalized. With this law, we risk fourteen years in prison.” Some Nigerian states also punish homosexuality with stoning to death, Valentina explains in a tone tinged with sadness.
Waves of nostalgia resurface. Valentina thinks of Nigeria: “I miss it sometimes, the landscapes, the warmth. What I miss most is the way people take care of one another. Nigerian society is less individualistic and more communal. The last time I set foot there was in 2014, the year the discriminatory law was adopted. More than ever, the oppression of queer and trans people is intensifying there. Any allusion, even the slightest, can lead to merciless prosecution. Unfortunately, justice fails them, and lets the police use and abuse their power to crack down on those who are perceived as queer.”
Au fur et à mesure que les souvenirs déf: As the memories unfold, Valentina painfully lets slip:
« L’histoire entre Marie et moi s’est te: “The story between Marie and me ended in discord. Before I left Nigeria, we had an argument. Her boyfriend suspected our lesbian relationship because of how close we were, and she claimed that I was obsessed with her. I understand the reasons for what she did now, but at the time, it hurt me deeply,” they confide.
Pendant ses années universitaires, une n: During their university years, tragic news reaches them from their country of origin: “Ma-Marie is no longer with us. When I heard the devastating news of her…suici…” Overcome with emotion, Valentina struggles to find the words. Then, looking away, they continue: “I knew instantly that she was gone because she couldn’t be herself, because she had no way of leaving Nigeria. She didn’t have the same luck I did.”
Ses larmes glissent, Valentina fixe le m: Tears slide down as Valentina stares at the wall, and for a full minute, they seem to disappear. After a deep breath, they explain: “The grief that overwhelms me is complicated, because Marie never fully accepted our truth. I carry the burden of our unshared story, unable to reveal the truth to the people who knew her. I know it would only make the wounds worse, adding a new layer of suffering to their already unbearable pain.”
Les yeux inondés, Valentina lance un sou: Eyes flooded with tears, Valentina smiles: “Now I realize that there are a lot of people I knew in Nigeria who are queer, and despite Marie’s tragedy, it makes me happy to know that some of them were able to leave the country and live their sexuality fully.”
Valentina a quitté son pays natal pour é: Valentina left their native country to escape the constraint of living a double life. Unfortunately, they find themself facing a similar situation in Canada. This time, it is not their gender or sexual identity that forces them to hide, but rather their immigration status. Because of an administrative oversight, the documents for renewing their study and work permit were lost by the educational institution they attended in Ontario, with disastrous consequences.
Tout cela s’est produit en même temps qu: All of this happened at the same time as the arrival of the COVID-19 pandemic, when everything was closed, and their renewal application was never filed. “Despite earning my master’s degree in Canada, I am refused any possibility of legally extending my stay or applying directly for permanent residency. I left everything so I wouldn’t have to hide, so I wouldn’t have to live in the shadows, and here I am living this nightmare again. I now find myself undocumented, still steeped in fear.”
Son statut, explique-t-iel, exacerbe ses: Their status, they explain, worsens their problems as a queer person, an immigrant and a member of a racialized community. “This situation has deeply deepened my depression, especially since I no longer have access to anything. I can’t even support myself, my rent, my groceries, I can’t even rent an apartment because I have no valid ID, and with<l1> the new Bill 31</l1>, there won’t even be lease transfers anymore. I sometimes feel imprisoned in my situation.”
Il ne lui reste qu’une lueur d’espoir. S: Only a glimmer of hope remains. Their last resort is to claim asylum and find refuge in Canada. Today, Valentina is beginning this process without knowing what the future holds.
Malgré la précarité de sa situation, iel: Despite the precariousness of their situation, they are quick to point out: “I know I’m still privileged compared to other undocumented people in this country, because I managed to find a way to work under the table. I’m also extremely lucky to be here in the first place, even though I’ve lost a lot of friends who weren’t so lucky.”
Cependant, iel soulève une problématique: However, they raise a problem concerning the resources allocated to queer BIPOC* people, which are limited, even more so when the needs of migrants, asylum seekers and refugees are included. Valentina believes community organizations suffer from a lack of funding. “There’s an overload of files and an obvious lack of staff. I’ve seen many workers leave because they were swamped with tasks and underpaid. It also means I constantly have to start my journey over, relive the same traumas, which makes my condition worse because I don’t have access to the health care I need,” they observe.
À plusieurs reprises, iel demande de l’a: On several occasions, they have asked for psychological support and help with their immigration process, but their requests have systematically been refused. “Given the scarcity of resources, these organizations tend to prioritize emergencies, such as people who are stranded abroad. That’s completely understandable, but it leaves few options for other situations, including mine,” says the exile understandingly.
<strong>« Quand on est en mode survie, o: “When you’re in survival mode, you don’t have the luxury of worrying about pronouns”
Au Canada, le manque de ressources des o: In Canada, organizations’ lack of resources is not the only obstacle Valentina faces. Even in queer circles, they can’t find comfort to ease their pain. Instead, they come up against normative discourses that ignore the diversity of their experiences.
Ayant vécu au Nigeria jusqu’à ses 17 ans: Having lived in Nigeria until they were 17, Valentina was unaware that Pride month existed. Once they had moved to Canada, they decided to attend the parade in Sudbury, where they lived before moving to Toronto and Montréal. “The people I knew in Sudbury at the time were mostly white. So I went with a friend who is a white, cisgender** gay man. As a Black, immigrant, queer person, I have a negative perception of experiences with the police. So I was surprised by their presence at the parade. I remember thinking: ‘Why are there police officers here? I thought Pride was a protest against the police,’” they recall.
La récupération du défilé de la Fierté p: The takeover of the Pride parade by brands and people in power.
Valentina fait référence ici aux émeutes: Valentina is referring here to the Stonewall riots, which took place on June 28, 1969. A rebellion was sparked by a violent police raid on the Stonewall Inn, a bar in the Greenwich Village neighbourhood of Manhattan. The bar, frequented mainly by transgender women and racialized gay men, was regularly the target of police brutality. The patrons finally fought back against this injustice, and the protest continued for six days, led by Black and Latina transgender women such as Marsha P. Johnson, Sylvia Rivera and Zazu Nova.
Valentina poursuit : « Les membres de Bl: Valentina continues: “The Black Lives Matter members who were at the march acted with determination, immediately interrupting the parade as soon as they spotted uniformed police officers. Their action highlighted the glaring contradiction and the importance of opposing the police institution even within an event like Pride. That gesture comforted me deeply.” A view their friend does not share. He made insensitive remarks, ignoring the experience of Black people in North America, including that of Valentina, who had to leave their country of origin out of fear of systemic violence and social repercussions, in order to live their life authentically. “At that moment, as he was complaining, I felt profoundly alone.”
Au fil du temps, Valentina a constaté qu: Over time, Valentina has found that their experience as a Black, migrant, queer person is often denied in public spaces. They have had to face a rise in racism and xenophobia within queer and trans communities. “I realized that in many white queer spaces, there is a latent racism, which shows up in questions about my legitimacy as a queer person of Nigerian origin and as someone belonging to a certain ethnic group,” explains Valentina in a tired tone.
Iel souligne notamment que dans les coll: They point out in particular that in collectives where white feminism*** is practised, Valentina is expected to live up to a preconceived version of queerness. “When I arrived, I tried to join 2SLGBTQIA+ groups, but I was expected to define my gender and sexual identity perfectly, including the pronouns to use, and to have exhaustive knowledge of all sexual orientations and gender identities,” they add. These expectations did not take into account the reality of Valentina and other queer racialized people. “When you’re in survival mode, you don’t have the luxury of worrying about pronouns, you’re constantly in a state of fear and flight. You live in secrecy, with deeply rooted shame. You don’t have time to negotiate how you want to be treated, you’re just trying to survive, to exist.”
L’immigrante explique que même au sein d: The immigrant explains that even within Black 2SLGBTQIA+ communities, there is exclusion and even xenophobia. “At first, I thought I could find my place within the Black queer and trans community, but we don’t share the same cultural baggage, or the same relationship to our Blackness.” They explain that in Canada, many Black people grew up in a country where the majority of the population is white, and therefore have to put a lot of effort and energy into preserving and proving their identities. “In these groups, I’m often told that I should wear my hair natural and avoid adopting a Canadian accent when I speak. But these demands don’t take into account the fact that I don’t have regular status, and that it risks marginalizing me even more,” they explain.
Valentina raconte une situation qu’iel a: Valentina recounts a situation they have experienced several times in racialized queer spaces that call themselves anti-racist. “There’s often this joke that young people from immigrant families make: they make fun of their African or Caribbean parents’ accents. These same people recommend that I use my natural accent, without understanding that by making fun of their parents and family, they’re also making fun of me. That kind of joke is insulting and reductive, especially when the jokes are about intelligence,” they explain. “Maybe it’s not racism, but it’s certainly xenophobia.”
D’ailleur, Valentina exprime que lorsqu’: Valentina also says that when they don’t fit established ideologies, they are punished and ostracized by their own presumed community: Black, African and queer. For example, when it comes to the ethnic and racial preferences of romantic partners. “I’ve often been told I shouldn’t be in relationships with white people to avoid fetishism and above all racism in intimate relationships, which is a recurring problem when we are people of colour. But once again, making that kind of decision isn’t part of my experience, and it’s imposed on me anyway. People can’t even understand that there was a time when I didn’t think I could be loved, when I didn’t think I could be in a relationship, when I didn’t think I could love without shame. I’m not in a position where I’m going to stop loving someone to avoid a potential problem,” says Valentina with determination.
<strong>« J’en ai assez de voir ma vie d: “I’m tired of seeing my life become a political statement”
Alors que les rues de Montréal se prépar: As the streets of Montréal prepare for this year’s Pride parade, Valentina explains that they have chosen not to attend anymore. “After my first two times, I decided not to take part in the Pride parade anymore, because it has become a highly capitalist spectacle. All these brands hand out condoms and whatnot, but they don’t hire people like us, immigrant, queer people of colour, for positions of power and influence, and they don’t lobby on our behalf when it matters,” they explain. Valentina looks at their T-shirt, which features a rock-metal version of Céline Dion, and breaks into a warm smile: “I now prefer to celebrate Pride with my friends and peers who have chosen to turn away from the official parade. It’s been taken over by companies that ride the rainbow to attract queers and make a profit.”
Un groupe de personnes racisées déçues e: A group of disappointed racialized people watching the Pride parade.
Deux mois après notre rencontre avec Val: Two months after our meeting with Valentina, a gentle farewell to the summer heat takes place. The first shivers of autumn brush over Montréal. In the second week of August, a scene takes shape: Montrealers adorn themselves with dazzling makeup, while others gather under a multitude of flags, symbols of their struggles and their hopes. As the excitement of the Pride parade builds, Valentina’s words resonate like a powerful whisper: “I’m tired of seeing my life reduced to a political statement. I want to be loved, simply. I don’t want every aspect of my existence to be reduced to a grand political story. I didn’t choose to be an activist, I was pushed down this path, just like others from similar backgrounds. You’re not born an activist, but you’re oppressed until you become one, and then you’re pushed to carry the banner of social justice,” says Valentina with assurance.
